speaker: Karen
text: Hello and welcome to the third lecture on the history of bridge engineering.

speaker: Karen
text: Today we follow one river crossing through nine centuries, from stone arches to modern suspension bridges.

speaker: Karen
text: Our case study is a crossing over a tidal estuary, which makes every design decision harder.

speaker: Karen
text: The water level changes by several metres twice a day, and the currents are strong.

speaker: Rishi
text: Let us begin with the oldest structure, because parts of it still stand.

speaker: Rishi
text: The oldest stone bridge still in use in the region was built in the year eleven forty.

speaker: Rishi
text: It has seven small arches, and each pier sits on a bed of timber piles driven into the mud.

speaker: Rishi
text: Those timber piles survived because they stayed wet and away from oxygen.

speaker: Rishi
text: When the river was dredged in the nineteenth century, two of the piers began to settle.

speaker: Karen
text: The next big change came with iron and then steel.

speaker: Karen
text: Iron allowed longer spans, but early iron bridges were brittle in cold weather.

speaker: Karen
text: Steel solved much of that, yet it brought its own problem.

speaker: Karen
text: The biggest enemy of steel bridges is corrosion, and most of it is caused by road salt in winter.

speaker: Karen
text: Salt water runs into the joints and sits there for months.

speaker: Rishi
text: Then came the material that changed everything, reinforced concrete.

speaker: Rishi
text: Concrete is strong when squeezed and weak when stretched, so steel bars carry the tension.

speaker: Rishi
text: It is cheap, it can be poured into almost any shape, and it does not need painting.

speaker: Rishi
text: Most of the short bridges you drive over every day are built this way.

speaker: Rishi
text: Even so, concrete cracks with time, and water in those cracks slowly attacks the steel inside.

speaker: Karen
text: Now to the star of the case study, the suspension bridge that opened in the nineteen sixties.

speaker: Karen
text: It has a main span of one thousand two hundred metres between the towers.

speaker: Karen
text: The two main cables are spun on site from thousands of individual steel wires.

speaker: Karen
text: Spinning the cables alone took almost a year.

speaker: Rishi
text: Long, light decks have a dangerous habit, they can start to oscillate in the wind.

speaker: Rishi
text: After wind tunnel testing, the engineers added slots along the deck to let the air pass through.

speaker: Rishi
text: Those slots break up the vortices that would otherwise make the deck swing.

speaker: Rishi
text: The same idea appears in almost every long span built since.

speaker: Karen
text: Keeping a bridge like this alive is a full time job.

speaker: Karen
text: Today it carries more than three hundred strain gauges that report how the steel is stretching.

speaker: Karen
text: Engineers also climb the cables in person, and a full inspection happens every six years.

speaker: Karen
text: Between inspections, the sensor data tells them where to look first.

speaker: Rishi
text: A few practical points before we stop.

speaker: Rishi
text: The field trip to the bridge is on Wednesday morning, and we meet at the train station.

speaker: Rishi
text: Wear sturdy shoes and bring a warm jacket, it is always windy on the deck.

speaker: Karen
text: And the reading for next week is chapter seven, on cable stayed bridges.

speaker: Karen
text: Thank you, and see you at the station.
